stem: The operations director of a national retailer tells an architect: "We want to use Claude in the returns process." No metrics, scope or current pain points have been stated. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Build a prototype returns agent with access to the order, refund and shipping tools so the director can react to something concrete rather than to a document.
options.why: Prototyping before the problem is defined optimises for a demo, not an outcome; the tools chosen encode assumptions nobody has validated and the prototype has no success criterion to be judged against.

options.text: Define the specific returns problem, its measured baseline and the target outcome with the director before proposing any design.
options.why: Translating a business problem into a solution starts with a scoped problem statement and a measurable baseline; every later design choice is judged against that target.

options.text: Select the most capable Claude model available so that whatever the returns use case turns out to be, model quality will not be the limiting factor.
options.why: Model choice is a downstream trade-off that depends on the task, latency and cost profile; choosing it first inverts the design process.

options.text: Index every returns-related document into a vector store so that retrieval is ready for whichever assistant is eventually built.
options.why: Building retrieval infrastructure before knowing whether the problem even needs document lookup is speculative work that may not address the real bottleneck.

explanation: The first architect deliverable is a scoped problem statement: which part of the process hurts, what the current numbers are, and what target defines success. Prototypes, model choice and infrastructure all follow from that, not the other way round.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (start simple); Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: An insurer's claims adjusters spend about 40 minutes per claim reading first-notice-of-loss (FNOL) forms, police reports and photos before they can even triage the claim. The claims VP wants "faster claims", but regulation requires a licensed adjuster to make every coverage decision. Which solution scope and success metric best translate this request?

options.text: Automate end-to-end claim adjudication with Claude, including the coverage decision, and measure success as the percentage of claims closed without any adjuster involvement.
options.why: Removing the adjuster from coverage decisions violates the regulatory constraint stated in the scenario, so this scope is not viable regardless of how efficient it would be.

options.text: Deploy a general Q&A assistant over the claims policy manual and measure success by adjuster satisfaction scores in a quarterly survey.
options.why: A policy Q&A tool does not address the identified bottleneck (reading and triaging FNOL evidence), and satisfaction is a weak proxy for the speed the VP asked for.

options.text: Have Claude generate a summary for every incoming claim and measure success by the number of summaries produced per adjuster per day.
options.why: Output volume is an activity metric, not an outcome metric; producing summaries proves nothing about whether triage got faster or whether adjusters trust them.

options.text: Have Claude extract key facts and draft a triage summary from the FNOL evidence for the adjuster; measure time-to-triage per claim against the 40-minute baseline.
options.why: This scopes Claude to the measured bottleneck, keeps the adjuster as decision-maker as regulation requires, and defines success as the outcome the VP cares about with a baseline to compare against.

explanation: A good translation names the specific step Claude will take over, keeps humans where regulation or risk requires them, and defines success as an outcome metric with a baseline (minutes per claim), not an activity metric such as summaries produced.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Anthropic — Building effective agents

stem: A hospital network wants Claude to cut the time clinicians spend writing discharge summaries. The chief medical information officer asks the architect for a solution definition before any build starts. Which two elements must that definition include? (Choose two.)

options.text: A measured baseline and target for the outcome, such as minutes per summary today versus the goal, plus the clinician sign-off rate the pilot must hold.
options.why: Without a baseline and target there is no way to know whether the solution worked; the sign-off rate protects against speed gains that clinicians reject.

options.text: Explicit boundaries on what Claude does: it drafts from the chart, a clinician reviews and signs, and nothing is written to the EHR without that sign-off.
options.why: Scope boundaries define where the model's output stops and human accountability starts, which is essential in a clinical setting.

options.text: A commitment to a specific Claude model tier so the finance team can forecast cost precisely from day one.
options.why: Model tier is a design decision to be validated against the task with evaluation; fixing it in the problem definition locks in a trade-off before the trade-off is understood.

options.text: A multi-agent architecture, because discharge summaries touch many specialties and each should have its own agent.
options.why: Architecture selection comes after the problem is defined; a single well-grounded call may be adequate, and multi-agent adds cost and complexity that nothing in the definition yet justifies.

options.text: A requirement that Claude reach 100% factual accuracy in testing before any clinician sees a draft.
options.why: An absolute accuracy bar is not measurable in practice and ignores that the design already relies on clinician review; the right bar is a target accuracy plus a review step.

explanation: A solution definition states the outcome and how it will be measured, and the boundaries of the model's role relative to the humans who stay accountable. Architecture and model choices come later, and absolute-accuracy requirements are neither measurable nor necessary when a human review step is part of the design.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A public benefits agency returns 30% of the 200,000 applications it receives each year because information is missing, and each return costs a caseworker about 20 minutes. Statute requires that eligibility be determined by a caseworker. The agency director asks for "a Claude solution to reduce rework". Which translation best fits every constraint?

options.text: An agent that reviews each application, determines eligibility and issues the decision letter, escalating only unusual cases to caseworkers.
options.why: Delegating eligibility determination to the model breaches the statutory requirement that a caseworker decide; escalating unusual cases does not cure that.

options.text: A public chatbot grounded in the benefits handbook that answers applicants' questions about the programme, measured by monthly chat volume.
options.why: General Q&A may or may not reduce incomplete submissions, and chat volume does not measure the stated problem; the link to the 30% return rate is speculative.

options.text: A pre-submission completeness check in which Claude compares each application against the required-evidence rules and tells the applicant exactly what is missing, measured by the first-time-complete rate.
options.why: This targets the specific cause of rework, leaves eligibility with caseworkers, and has a direct outcome metric that maps to the 20-minute-per-return cost.

options.text: Replace the application form with a conversational intake in which Claude interviews the applicant and fills in the form on their behalf, measured by applicant satisfaction.
options.why: A full intake redesign is a large, hard-to-measure change with new accuracy and accessibility risks; it does not isolate the missing-information problem the director named.

explanation: Scope the solution to the measured cause (incomplete submissions), keep the regulated decision with humans, and choose a metric that moves directly with the business cost. Bigger redesigns and general assistants may be valuable later but do not translate this request.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Anthropic — Building effective agents

stem: A SaaS vendor's CEO says: "Customers churn because onboarding is hard; build an AI assistant." The architect's discovery finds that 60% of churned accounts never completed integration setup, and support tickets raised during setup cluster around three recurring configuration errors. Which solution translation makes the strongest business case?

options.text: A guided-setup assistant that checks the customer's integration configuration and walks them through the three recurring fixes, measured by 14-day integration completion against a control cohort.
options.why: It targets the root cause discovery uncovered, is scoped tightly enough to build and evaluate quickly, and the metric links directly to the churn driver.

options.text: A general product assistant with retrieval over the full documentation set and every help-centre article, available on every page of the product, measured by customer satisfaction with the assistant's answers.
options.why: A broad assistant dilutes effort across the whole product, and its satisfaction metric does not tell the CEO whether onboarding completion or churn moved.

options.text: An agent with credentials to each customer's environment that detects configuration problems and applies the fixes automatically without asking, measured by the number of fixes applied per week.
options.why: Autonomous writes into customer environments carry blast-radius and trust risks that are unjustified for a first solution when guided fixes address the same errors.

options.text: A six-month discovery programme interviewing churned customers to confirm the cause before committing to any build, measured by interviews completed.
options.why: Discovery already surfaced a specific, measurable cause; further open-ended research delays value without changing the diagnosis.

explanation: Translate the business problem into the narrowest solution that attacks the evidenced root cause, and define success with a metric that moves with the business outcome and can be compared against a control. Breadth, autonomy and further research all weaken the case here.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (start simple); Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A bank's fraud-operations sponsor wants to "use Claude to catch more fraud". Discovery finds: an existing ML model scores every card transaction in under 50 ms with high recall; analysts spend about 25 minutes per alert gathering evidence from six systems and writing a disposition narrative; and the regulator requires that every disposition be made by a human and be explainable from documented evidence. Which translation satisfies all of these constraints?

options.text: Replace the ML scorer with a Claude classifier so that reasoning about transaction context raises recall further.
options.why: An LLM call cannot meet the sub-50 ms real-time budget of the scoring path, and the existing model already has high recall; this attacks the wrong bottleneck.

options.text: Run Claude alongside the ML model as a second scorer on every transaction and merge the two scores into one alert threshold.
options.why: It doubles real-time cost on a path that is not the constraint and produces a probabilistic score the regulator cannot trace to documented evidence for a human decision.

options.text: Have Claude assemble the evidence package from the six systems and draft the disposition narrative with references, with the analyst confirming the decision; measure alert handling time and analyst throughput.
options.why: The measured bottleneck is analyst time per alert, not detection; this design keeps the human decision and evidence trail the regulator requires while quantifying the gain.

options.text: Let Claude auto-close low-risk alerts and hand only high-risk alerts to analysts, measuring the reduction in the analyst queue size.
options.why: Auto-closing alerts is a disposition made by the model, which the regulator prohibits; queue reduction achieved that way cannot be deployed.

explanation: "Catch more fraud" is the sponsor's phrasing, but discovery shows detection is already strong and the bottleneck is analyst time per alert. The correct translation targets that bottleneck, respects the real-time and human-decision constraints, and measures the outcome that actually changes.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Anthropic — Building effective agents

stem: A legal-operations team at an insurer uses Claude to summarise vendor contracts. Reviewers edit roughly 20% of summaries before filing them, but the edited versions are stored only in the document system and the pipeline never sees them. Which addition completes the input → processing → output architecture?

options.text: A retry that automatically re-runs the summary with different sampling settings whenever a reviewer edits it, replacing the reviewer's version with the new draft.
options.why: Re-running after the fact produces a second output nobody asked for and learns nothing from what the reviewer changed.

options.text: A token-usage dashboard so the team can see how much each contract summary costs.
options.why: Cost visibility is useful operationally, but it does not feed reviewer corrections back into improving the output.

options.text: An upgrade to a larger model tier to bring the 20% edit rate down.
options.why: Changing the model without measuring what reviewers fix is a guess; the edit rate might drop, rise or shift without anyone knowing why.

options.text: A feedback loop that stores each reviewer's edited version next to the original draft and feeds the pairs into the evaluation set run before prompt changes.
options.why: An end-to-end architecture closes the loop: human corrections become labelled data that drive evaluation and iteration of prompts, retrieval and model choice.

explanation: Input, processing and output are only three quarters of the design. The feedback loop turns production outcomes (reviewer edits, evaluation results) into an evidence base for iteration, which is what keeps a system improving after launch.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A retailer generates product descriptions for 50,000 SKUs every night from supplier feeds. There is no latency requirement, every description must conform to a JSON schema before it can be published, and merchandisers reject about 3% of drafts for tone. Which end-to-end design fits best?

options.text: Submit the nightly run through the Message Batches API, validate every output against the schema in code, route schema failures and a sample of passes to a merchandiser review queue, and add rejected drafts to a regression evaluation set.
options.why: Batches suit large asynchronous jobs; deterministic schema validation gates publication; a review queue plus regression set gives the feedback loop that reduces the 3% over time.

options.text: Stream each description to the merchandising UI in real time as it is generated so merchandisers can approve every item as it appears, then publish approved items immediately.
options.why: Streaming solves perceived latency for interactive users, which this nightly pipeline does not have, and it puts 50,000 approvals on people instead of a sampled review.

options.text: Run one agent per SKU that reads the supplier feed, writes the description, decides whether it meets the tone guide and publishes it directly to the storefront.
options.why: Per-SKU agents add cost and non-determinism to a fixed, predictable task and remove the deterministic validation gate before publication.

options.text: Send all 50,000 SKUs in a single request and ask Claude to return one JSON array for the whole catalogue, then publish the array once it parses.
options.why: A single request cannot hold the full catalogue and would produce an unverifiable monolithic output with no per-item gating.

explanation: Match the processing stage to the job's shape (asynchronous bulk work suits Batches), gate output with deterministic validation, and build the feedback loop from human rejections so the system improves. Real-time or agentic designs add cost without serving any stated need.
reference: Claude docs — Batch processing; Structured outputs

stem: A hospital network routes incoming patient-portal messages with Claude, assigning each to one of five triage categories before a nurse handles it. The architect must design the feedback stage. Which two mechanisms give the strongest improvement loop? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask Claude to output a confidence score with each category and log the average confidence as the system's accuracy metric.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not calibrated accuracy; averaging it measures how sure the model sounds, not how often it is right.

options.text: Record every case where the nurse changes the assigned category and track the override rate per category as an ongoing accuracy signal.
options.why: Nurse overrides are real corrections from the accountable human; the override rate per category is a direct, continuously available measure of triage quality.

options.text: Send each message to two different models and keep whichever answers first.
options.why: Racing models optimises latency, not correctness, and produces no signal about which category was right.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so the model explores more categories and learns from the variety.
options.why: Temperature changes output randomness; the model does not learn from its own production outputs, so this only adds noise.

options.text: Periodically sample triaged messages, stratified by category, for clinical review, and add every disagreement to the evaluation set that runs before prompt changes.
options.why: Stratified sampling catches errors the nurse did not override, and adding disagreements to the eval set turns findings into a regression guard.

explanation: Feedback loops need real ground truth: corrections from the accountable human in the flow and a stratified sampled review that catches silent errors. Both feed an evaluation set that gates future changes. Self-reported confidence, model racing and temperature changes are not feedback mechanisms.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Anthropic — Demystifying evals for AI agents

stem: A public records office receives information requests by email, web form and scanned letters. Claude classifies each request and drafts an acknowledgement that is written into the case-management system. Auditors must be able to reproduce, months later, exactly why any given acknowledgement was produced. Which architecture satisfies that requirement?

options.text: Send each raw email, form payload or scan directly to Claude as it arrives, and store only the final acknowledgement text in the case system.
options.why: Without the exact input, prompt and model version, no one can reproduce the output; storing only the result breaks the audit trail.

options.text: Normalise every channel into a canonical request record at ingestion, version the prompt and pin the model ID, persist the exact context and response per case, and write the acknowledgement through a validated schema.
options.why: Canonical input, versioned prompt, pinned model and persisted context make every output reproducible; schema-validated writes keep the output stage deterministic.

options.text: Give an agent direct database access to write acknowledgements and rely on the database's transaction log as the audit record of what was decided and why.
options.why: A transaction log records what was written, not the prompt, input and model that produced it, and direct agent writes remove the validation gate.

options.text: Keep prompts under version control but skip request-level logging to reduce storage costs, since the prompt history is enough to explain any output.
options.why: Prompt history without the per-request input and response cannot explain any specific acknowledgement; reproducibility needs the actual context.

explanation: Reproducibility is an architectural property: normalise inputs, version prompts and models, persist the exact context and output per case, and make the output stage a validated write. Logs of the result alone or of the prompt alone are not enough.
reference: Claude docs — Structured outputs; Models overview (model IDs and versioning)

stem: A bank runs a customer-facing Claude assistant that must answer within a p95 of 3 seconds. Compliance also requires that every transcript be reviewed for disclosure violations within 24 hours, and review findings must improve the assistant. The architect is designing the processing and feedback stages. Which two design choices are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the full compliance review inline before each reply is returned, so no non-compliant response ever reaches a customer.
options.why: An extra full review call on the critical path threatens the 3-second p95, and compliance asked for 24-hour review, not synchronous blocking; lightweight inline guardrails are a separate matter.

options.text: Serve the interactive path with streaming responses and a tightly scoped context, and run the transcript review as a separate asynchronous job using the Message Batches API.
options.why: Separating the latency-sensitive path from the bulk review lets each be optimised for its own constraint; batches suit a 24-hour window at lower cost.

options.text: Run both the customer replies and the compliance review through the nightly batch job to keep the architecture simple.
options.why: A batched customer reply cannot meet an interactive latency target; the two workloads have different constraints and need different paths.

options.text: Feed each confirmed violation from the review into a labelled evaluation set that runs against the assistant's prompt before any change is released.
options.why: This closes the feedback loop compliance asked for: findings become regression tests that guard future prompt and model changes.

options.text: Address each violation by appending a new rule to the system prompt and redeploying immediately without other testing.
options.why: Prompt patches without evaluation accumulate into a brittle prompt and give no evidence that the fix works or that it broke nothing else.

options.text: Store transcripts only when a customer complains, to minimise data retention.
options.why: Compliance requires every transcript to be reviewed; selective retention makes the review incomplete and the feedback loop unrepresentative.

explanation: Design the processing stage per workload constraint (streaming for interactive latency, Batches for bulk asynchronous review) and make the feedback stage concrete: review findings become evaluation cases that gate changes. Inline full review, uniform batching and untested prompt patches each break one of the stated requirements.
reference: Claude docs — Streaming Messages; Batch processing; Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: An insurer's claims pipeline extracts invoice line items and totals with Claude, validates them and hands them to adjusters, who approve payment. Audits show 2% of extractions contain a wrong amount that passed unnoticed because adjusters trust the extracted numbers, and the regulator now requires evidence for every approved figure. Adjusters cannot re-key every field, and the sponsor will not accept slower approvals. Which architecture change best closes the loop?

options.text: Add an evaluator step in which a second Claude call independently re-extracts each invoice and flags any disagreement with the first extraction to the adjuster for a decision.
options.why: A second model pass reduces some errors but still gives adjusters no evidence to verify against, and correlated errors between two model calls pass unflagged; it does not meet the evidence requirement.

options.text: Switch extraction to a larger model, keep the rest of the pipeline unchanged, and re-measure the error rate after a month of production traffic.
options.why: Model size may or may not move the 2% and provides neither evidence for approved figures nor a mechanism to catch the errors that remain.

options.text: Require adjusters to re-enter every extracted amount from the source invoice before approval so that each figure has a human-verified record.
options.why: Full manual re-keying satisfies evidence but violates the constraints that adjusters cannot re-key and approvals must not slow down; it also discards the value of extraction.

options.text: Return each amount with a citation to its source location on the invoice, add deterministic cross-field checks (line items summing to totals), and route flagged cases plus a stratified random sample to adjuster verification whose corrections feed the evaluation set.
options.why: Citations give evidence per figure and make spot checks fast, deterministic checks catch arithmetic errors without model cost, and sampled verification feeding evals provides the measurement loop the pipeline lacked.

explanation: Closing the loop means output that carries provenance, deterministic gates where the check is mechanical, calibrated human verification (flagged plus stratified sample) rather than universal re-keying, and corrections flowing back into evaluation. A second model pass or a bigger model addresses symptoms without evidence or measurement.
reference: Claude docs — Citations; Structured outputs; Increase output consistency

stem: A bank receives customer emails that fall into six well-understood categories (address change, card dispute, statement request, and so on). Each category has its own handling prompt and tools, and the handling never overlaps. Which pattern from Anthropic's workflow catalogue fits?

options.text: Routing: a classifier call assigns each email to a category and hands it to that category's prompt and tools.
options.why: Routing is designed for inputs that fall into distinct, known categories that are best handled separately; it keeps each downstream prompt focused.

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts a reply and a second call critiques it until the draft passes.
options.why: Evaluator-optimizer is for iterative refinement against clear criteria, not for dispatching inputs to different handlers.

options.text: An autonomous agent that reads each email and decides which tools to use and in what order.
options.why: An agent's flexibility is unnecessary when the categories and handling paths are already known; it adds cost and variability.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a lead agent breaks each email into subtasks, delegates them to parallel worker agents and merges their results into a reply.
options.why: Orchestrator-workers suits tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance, not a fixed classification into known handlers.

explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialised follow-up task, which keeps each handler's prompt simple and lets categories be tuned independently. It is the right choice when the categories are distinct and known in advance.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (routing)

stem: A retailer's marketing team uses Claude to draft campaign copy that must comply with a written 12-rule brand guideline. Today a copywriter reviews each draft, sends back comments, and the loop repeats two or three times. The team wants to automate the refinement while keeping the same quality bar. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Parallelization with voting: generate five drafts at once and keep the one that most of the drafts resemble.
options.why: Voting over drafts selects for consensus, not for compliance with the specific rules; nothing checks the rules.

options.text: Prompt chaining: draft the copy, then translate it, then format it for each channel in a fixed sequence.
options.why: A fixed chain performs transformations, but the need here is iterative correction against criteria, which a linear chain does not provide.

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, a second evaluates the draft against the 12 rules and returns feedback, looping until it passes or a round limit is hit.
options.why: The refinement loop has clear evaluation criteria and evidence that iterative feedback improves the output, which is exactly when evaluator-optimizer pays off.

options.text: An autonomous agent with web search that researches the brand's public presence and past campaigns, then rewrites the copy in a loop until it judges the result satisfactory.
options.why: Open-ended autonomy and web search add cost and unpredictability; the criteria are already written down, so no research is needed.

explanation: Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement measurably helps, mirroring what the human reviewer did. Bound the loop with a maximum number of rounds so cost stays predictable.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (evaluator-optimizer)

stem: A SaaS vendor wants a "Summarise this ticket" button in its support console. On each click the system fetches the ticket, its last five comments and the customer's plan tier, and Claude returns a short summary. Volume is high and the button must feel instant. Which architecture is the best fit?

options.text: An agent that decides which tickets and comments to read, calls tools in a loop and stops when it judges the summary complete.
options.why: The inputs are already known and fixed per click; an agentic loop adds turns, latency and cost to decide something the code already knows.

options.text: A single augmented LLM call with the retrieved ticket data in context and a structured output schema for the summary.
options.why: When the inputs are fixed and the task is one predictable transformation, a single well-grounded call is the simplest, fastest and cheapest design that meets the need.

options.text: An orchestrator that splits the ticket into comment-level subtasks handled by parallel worker agents and merges their summaries.
options.why: Five comments do not need parallel workers; the merge step adds latency and cost and the summaries lose cross-comment coherence.

options.text: An evaluator-optimizer loop that drafts the summary and refines it until a second evaluator call approves it.
options.why: There are no stated quality criteria demanding iteration and the button must feel instant; extra rounds directly harm the latency target.

explanation: Start with the simplest design that meets the requirement. An augmented LLM (a single call with retrieval and structure) handles a fixed-input, single-step task at the lowest latency and cost; workflows and agents are justified only when the task needs them.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (the augmented LLM; start simple)

stem: A city permits office wants Claude to help review building-permit applications. Every application goes through the same four steps: completeness check, zoning-rule check, fee calculation and drafting the response letter. About 15% of applications need a clarifying question to the applicant before the zoning check can finish. Auditors need a reproducible path for every application and the budget per application is fixed. The lead developer proposes an autonomous agent "for flexibility". Which design should the architect recommend instead?

options.text: Accept the agent proposal but add a turn limit and a token budget so the cost per application stays bounded.
options.why: A turn limit caps cost but the step order still varies per run, which fails the auditors' need for a reproducible path when the path is already known.

options.text: A single augmented LLM call that performs all four checks and drafts the letter in one pass with a structured output.
options.why: Collapsing four steps loses the gates between them, and a one-pass design cannot pause for the 15% that need applicant input.

options.text: An orchestrator-workers system with one worker agent per check, so the four checks run in parallel and finish sooner.
options.why: Fee calculation and the response letter depend on the completeness and zoning outcomes, so the checks are not independent; parallel agents add coordination cost for no gain.

options.text: A prompt-chain workflow with programmatic gates between the four steps and a defined exception path that pauses the chain, sends the clarifying question, and resumes when the applicant replies.
options.why: The steps are known and ordered, so a workflow gives reproducibility and fixed cost; the exception is a predictable branch, not a reason for open-ended autonomy.

explanation: A predictable exception (a clarifying question in 15% of cases) is handled by an explicit branch in a workflow, not by abandoning the workflow for an agent. Workflows win where the path is known, auditability matters and cost must be fixed.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (prompt chaining; when to use workflows vs agents)

stem: An architect maintains a workflow that processes engineering change requests. Stakeholders keep asking to "make it an agent". Which two conditions would genuinely justify replacing the workflow with an agent? (Choose two.)

options.text: The number and order of steps depend on what each tool call reveals, so no fixed sequence covers the realistic cases.
options.why: When the path cannot be predicted in advance, a model that plans its own next step based on tool results is the pattern that fits; that is the defining case for agents.

options.text: The team wants to reduce per-request cost and latency below what the workflow achieves.
options.why: Agents typically cost more and take longer than a fixed workflow because they spend turns deciding what to do; they are chosen for capability, not economy.

options.text: The compliance team needs an identical, reproducible execution path for every request.
options.why: Reproducibility is a strength of workflows; agents vary their path per run, which is the opposite of what compliance is asking for.

options.text: The task runs in an environment where the agent gets reliable feedback on its progress, such as tests, checks or tool results it can verify.
options.why: Agents work well only when the environment lets them observe the outcome of each action; without ground truth they drift, so this is a precondition for agentic autonomy.

options.text: One step of the current workflow fails 10% of the time and the team wants the system to try harder.
options.why: A flaky step is fixed by improving that step (better prompt, validation, retry); turning the whole pipeline agentic spreads unpredictability everywhere without addressing the fault.

explanation: Move to an agent when the path is genuinely unpredictable and the environment gives verifiable feedback. Wanting lower cost, reproducibility or a fix for one weak step are reasons to keep and improve the workflow.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (agents; when to use)

stem: A bank's operations team resolves trade breaks. Analysis of a year of cases shows 80% follow one of four known resolution procedures, while 20% need open-ended investigation across settlement, custody and reference-data systems. Internal audit requires the resolution path for procedural cases to be reproducible. The sponsor's target is specifically to cut analyst time on the 20% investigative cases, and the token budget is tight. Which design meets every constraint?

options.text: A routing step classifies each break; the four known procedures run as deterministic workflows, and the investigative cases go to a bounded agent with a turn limit and analyst sign-off.
options.why: Routing preserves reproducibility and low cost for the 80%, while a bounded agent addresses the sponsor's actual target on the 20%; each part uses the pattern its predictability warrants.

options.text: A single agent handles every break with all three systems as tools, since one design is easier to maintain and the agent can follow the procedures when they apply.
options.why: Running the 80% procedural cases through an agent forfeits reproducibility and multiplies token spend on cases that need neither, breaking two stated constraints.

options.text: Workflows for the four procedures, with the 20% investigative cases queued directly to analysts exactly as they are handled today.
options.why: This meets audit and budget constraints but does nothing for the sponsor's stated target, which is analyst time on the investigative cases.

options.text: An orchestrator that spawns a worker agent per system (settlement, custody, reference data) for every break and merges their findings into a resolution.
options.why: Spawning parallel workers for every break applies the most expensive pattern uniformly, including to the procedural 80%, and offers no reproducible path for audit.

explanation: Hybrid designs are common: route by predictability, use workflows where the path is known (auditable, cheap) and a bounded agent only where investigation is genuinely open-ended. The sponsor's target rules out leaving the hard cases fully manual, and the audit and budget constraints rule out agents for everything.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (routing; agents)

stem: A SaaS vendor wants a weekly competitive brief covering 30 competitors. For each competitor the work is the same: read recent announcements, pricing pages and reviews, then summarise changes. The threads are independent and each produces far more raw material than the final brief needs. Which design fits?

options.text: One agent that researches the 30 competitors one after another in a single long conversation.
options.why: A single sequential agent takes far longer and its context fills with raw material from earlier competitors, degrading the later ones.

options.text: A prompt chain that summarises all 30 competitors in one call, then formats the result in a second call, adds an executive headline in a third and emails the brief.
options.why: One call cannot hold the raw material for 30 competitors, and a chain gives no parallelism for independent threads.

options.text: A coordinator that dispatches one subagent per competitor in parallel, each in its own context, and synthesises their condensed findings.
options.why: Independent, parallelisable threads with heavy intermediate output are the textbook case for orchestrator-workers: parallelism cuts wall-clock time and context isolation keeps the coordinator focused.

options.text: Four peer agents that message each other freely and stop when they agree the brief is complete.
options.why: Peer agents without a coordinator have no owner for decomposition or synthesis, which leads to loops and unclear ownership of the final output.

explanation: Multi-agent designs pay off when tasks parallelise and when the raw context exceeds what one agent should hold. A coordinator owns the decomposition and the final synthesis; workers explore independently and return compressed findings.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A bank's KYC team runs a three-step document check: extract fields from the identity document, compare them with the application form, and flag mismatches. A vendor proposes rebuilding it as a multi-agent system with an extractor agent, a comparison agent and a supervisor agent, "for robustness". What should the architect conclude?

options.text: Accept, because separating concerns across agents improves accuracy and makes each agent easier to test in isolation.
options.why: Separation of concerns can be achieved with separate prompts in a workflow; multiple agents add coordination overhead and token cost without an accuracy mechanism.

options.text: Decline: the steps are fixed, sequential and share one small context, so a prompt chain with a deterministic comparison step gives the same separation at far lower cost.
options.why: Multi-agent architectures earn their overhead only when work parallelises or exceeds one context; a three-step sequential check meets neither test, and field comparison should be code, not a model.

options.text: Accept, but replace the supervisor with a shared message bus so the extractor and comparison agents coordinate directly, which removes the supervisor's token cost and latency.
options.why: Removing the coordinator makes the multi-agent design worse, not cheaper; the underlying problem is that multiple agents are unwarranted here.

options.text: Decline, because multi-agent systems are only appropriate for research and content-generation use cases, not regulated processes.
options.why: Multi-agent designs suit any domain where subtasks are independent and parallel or context-heavy; the reason to decline here is the task's shape, not its domain.

explanation: Multi-agent systems burn many times more tokens than a single call (Anthropic reports roughly 15x versus a chat) and add coordination failure modes. They are justified when work parallelises or when the total context exceeds one window, not to make a small sequential pipeline feel more robust.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system; Building effective agents

stem: A hospital network's architect is reviewing proposals for Claude-based systems and must decide which ones justify a multi-agent design. Which two characteristics of a task indicate that multi-agent orchestration is likely to pay off? (Choose two.)

options.text: The task must minimise total token spend per run.
options.why: Multi-agent runs cost several times more tokens than single-agent runs, so cost minimisation argues against them.

options.text: The task consists of tightly coupled edits to one shared artefact in a strict order.
options.why: Tightly coupled sequential work is hard to split; parallel agents editing shared state create conflicts and lost context.

options.text: The task splits into independent lines of enquiry that can run at the same time.
options.why: Parallel, independent subtasks are the main source of multi-agent speed and breadth gains.

options.text: Each response must return within two seconds for a simple lookup.
options.why: Coordination and subagent turns add latency; a simple low-latency lookup is best served by one call.

options.text: The material that must be examined far exceeds what one context window can hold, and only condensed findings are needed at the end.
options.why: Giving each subagent its own context window and returning compressed results is how multi-agent systems scale past a single context.

options.text: The team wants each agent to adopt a different persona to make the output more varied.
options.why: Personas are a prompting choice, not an architectural reason; variety of voice does not require separate agents.

explanation: The two structural signals for multi-agent designs are parallelisable independent subtasks and context that exceeds one window. Cost, latency for simple tasks and tightly coupled work point the other way, and stylistic variety is not an architectural driver.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A retailer's catalogue-enrichment system uses a coordinator and eight worker agents, each enriching a slice of products from supplier data. Workers write their results directly into the catalogue database. In production, two workers sometimes enrich the same product with conflicting attributes, and a failed worker leaves half-written records. Which change best fixes the design?

options.text: Add an instruction to each worker's prompt to query the database before writing, skip any product that another worker has already touched, and roll back its own writes if it fails.
options.why: A prompt instruction is probabilistic and racy; two workers can both check and both write, and a worker that crashes mid-write cannot run its own rollback.

options.text: Run the eight workers one after another so that no two workers can ever touch the same product at the same time.
options.why: Sequential workers eliminate the conflict at the cost of the parallelism that justified the multi-agent design in the first place.

options.text: Give every worker the full product catalogue in its context so it can see what the other workers are doing.
options.why: Workers cannot see each other's in-flight writes from a context snapshot, and loading the whole catalogue into every worker defeats context isolation.

options.text: Have workers return structured results to the coordinator, which owns partitioning, deduplicates and merges them, and performs the writes as validated transactions.
options.why: The coordinator owns decomposition and synthesis; giving it the side effects makes writes atomic and conflict-free while workers stay parallel and stateless.

explanation: In orchestrator-worker designs, the orchestrator owns the decomposition, the synthesis and, in most cases, the side effects. Workers that write shared state directly reintroduce concurrency and partial-failure problems that prompts cannot solve.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (orchestrator-workers); How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A public agency's research assistant uses a lead agent that spawns subagents. Cost analysis shows it spawns 15 to 20 subagents for almost every query, including simple fact checks such as "what is the filing deadline for form 12?", and the token bill is fifteen times that of the old single-call assistant. Which change should the architect make first?

options.text: Give the lead agent explicit scaling rules: simple fact checks use one agent with a few tool calls, comparisons use a few subagents, and only broad research spawns many subagents with divided responsibilities.
options.why: Multi-agent effort should scale with query complexity; embedding scaling heuristics in the lead agent's prompt is the documented fix for over-spawning and directly cuts wasted tokens.

options.text: Cap every subagent's context at 2,000 tokens and its tool calls at three so that each subagent costs a fixed small amount regardless of the query.
options.why: A hard cap starves subagents on the queries that genuinely need depth and does nothing about spawning 15 subagents for a trivial question.

options.text: Replace the lead agent with a smaller, cheaper model tier and keep the subagent count and subagent model unchanged to preserve research quality.
options.why: A cheaper lead agent lowers one line item but leaves the structural waste of spawning many workers per trivial query, and a weaker planner tends to decompose worse.

options.text: Remove the multi-agent design entirely and return to the single-call assistant for every query, since the cost increase cannot be justified.
options.why: Some queries are broad enough to benefit from parallel subagents; discarding the capability throws away value instead of governing when it is used.

explanation: Lead agents over-spawn unless told how to scale effort. The fix is explicit heuristics in the orchestrator prompt that map query complexity to the number of subagents and tool calls, reserving expensive parallel research for queries that need it.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system (scale effort to query complexity)

stem: A bank is designing a multi-agent due-diligence system. Requirements: a run covering one counterparty must finish within 10 minutes; every finding in the final report must cite its source; subagents fail intermittently on rate-limited external sources; and the lead agent's context regularly overflows when it collects raw subagent output. Which three design decisions address these requirements? (Choose three.)

options.text: The lead agent plans the decomposition, runs subagents in parallel with distinct objectives and output formats, and each subagent returns condensed findings with source references rather than raw pages.
options.why: Parallel subagents with condensed outputs meet the time budget and stop the lead agent's context from overflowing, and carrying source references makes citation possible.

options.text: Give every subagent the lead agent's full conversation history so that it has the maximum possible context for its task.
options.why: Copying the full history into every subagent multiplies token cost, does nothing for the overflow problem and is not how subagents should receive a scoped brief.

options.text: Persist each subagent's results outside the conversation context, so a failed subagent can be retried from its last checkpoint without restarting the whole run.
options.why: Durable intermediate state and resumable retries are the standard answer to intermittent subagent failures in long-running multi-agent runs.

options.text: Run subagents strictly one after another so that their failures are easier to observe and debug.
options.why: Sequential execution makes the 10-minute budget unreachable and gives up the parallelism that justified the design.

options.text: Add a final citation step that maps each claim in the synthesised report back to its source before delivery.
options.why: Citation is best handled as a dedicated pass over the finished report with the collected sources, ensuring every finding is attributed.

options.text: Let subagents write their findings directly into the final report document as each one completes.
options.why: Uncoordinated writes bypass the lead agent's synthesis, producing an inconsistent narrative and unresolved conflicts between subagents.

explanation: Production multi-agent systems separate planning and synthesis (lead agent) from parallel scoped exploration (subagents returning condensed findings), persist state so partial failures are resumable, and handle citations as a final pass over the synthesised output.
reference: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A compliance team needs to compare a 400-page regulatory rulebook against its internal policies and list the gaps. The rulebook is far larger than what fits comfortably alongside the policies in one request. What is the most appropriate first decomposition?

options.text: Submit the entire rulebook and all internal policies in a single request and instruct Claude to be thorough, read every section in order and list every gap it finds without skipping anything.
options.why: The combined material exceeds a practical context budget, and "be thorough" does not change what the model can attend to.

options.text: Ask Claude to generate a one-paragraph summary of the rulebook first, then compare that summary with the policies in a second call.
options.why: A one-paragraph summary discards the specific obligations that gap analysis depends on; the compression is far too lossy.

options.text: Let an agent decide for itself which pages of the rulebook to read based on the titles of the internal policies.
options.why: An unguided agent may skip sections; the rulebook has a natural structure that gives a complete, predictable partition without relying on model judgement.

options.text: Split the rulebook along its own chapters or sections, run the gap check per section against the relevant policies, then merge the findings.
options.why: Decomposing by data boundary uses the document's natural units, keeps each call within context, and makes coverage complete and auditable before results are aggregated.

explanation: When the input is too large, decompose along its natural data boundaries (sections, records, accounts), process each unit independently and aggregate. This keeps each call focused and lets you verify that every unit was covered.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (parallelization: sectioning); Claude docs — Long context prompting tips

stem: A law firm uses one large prompt that asks Claude to read a commercial lease, identify risky clauses, rate each clause's severity and draft redline suggestions. Quality is inconsistent: severity ratings are often wrong for clauses the model summarised correctly, and redlines sometimes reference clauses that were never identified. Which decomposition most directly improves this?

options.text: Break the task into sequential steps (extract clauses as structured data, then rate severity per clause, then draft redlines for high-severity clauses) with checks between steps.
options.why: Decomposing by step turns one hard task into simpler calls, each easier to get right and to evaluate, and the gates stop errors (such as redlines for unidentified clauses) from propagating.

options.text: Keep the single prompt but add ten worked examples of correctly rated clauses with matching redlines, and a reminder to only redline clauses it has identified, so the model calibrates its ratings.
options.why: Few-shot examples help calibrate one judgement, but they do not fix the structural problem of one call juggling extraction, rating and drafting at once.

options.text: Run the same prompt five times and keep the majority answer for each clause's severity and the most common redline.
options.why: Voting reduces random variance but not the systematic difficulty of doing three interdependent tasks in one pass; it also multiplies cost.

options.text: Move to a larger model and ask it to reason step by step within the single call before producing the final ratings and redlines.
options.why: Chain-of-thought inside one call may help somewhat, but the errors are inter-step consistency failures that explicit intermediate outputs and checks address directly.

explanation: Decomposition by step (prompt chaining) trades a little latency for higher accuracy: each call does one thing, produces structured intermediate output, and code can validate it before the next step runs.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (prompt chaining); Claude docs — Chain complex prompts

stem: An insurer's underwriting desk wants Claude to assess complex life-insurance applications from three angles: medical history, financial disclosure and legal or regulatory flags. Underwriters insist that the three assessments be formed independently so that one perspective does not anchor another, and then be reconciled. Which decomposition matches this requirement?

options.text: One generalist prompt that covers all three angles in a single pass and produces a combined recommendation with a clearly labelled section per angle and an overall score.
options.why: A single pass lets the model's reading of one area colour the others, which is the anchoring the underwriters want to avoid.

options.text: A sequential chain in which the medical assessment is passed into the financial assessment, which is passed into the legal assessment.
options.why: Passing each output into the next assessment deliberately anchors later steps on earlier ones, violating the independence requirement.

options.text: Three parallel calls, each with a specialist prompt and only the evidence for its angle, followed by a synthesis step that reconciles the three assessments.
options.why: Decomposition by expertise runs specialist perspectives in isolation (sectioning), so each is formed independently, and the synthesis step handles reconciliation explicitly.

options.text: An agent that reads the application and chooses which angle to examine first based on what looks most material to the risk.
options.why: An agent choosing its own order still reasons in one context across angles, so assessments influence each other; it also makes the process less reproducible.

explanation: Decomposing by expertise means running independent specialist prompts, often in parallel, each with its own scoped evidence, then reconciling in a synthesis step. It preserves independent judgement and makes each perspective separately evaluable.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (parallelization: sectioning)

stem: A hospital network must compute 12 quality indicators (for example, documented medication reconciliation within 24 hours) across 2,000 patient records for a quarterly report. Records are independent, indicators require reading free-text notes, and the report needs network-wide totals per indicator. Which two decomposition decisions are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Decompose by indicator: for each of the 12 indicators, send all 2,000 records in one request and ask for that indicator's total.
options.why: Two thousand records do not fit in one request, and mixing many patients' notes into one context invites cross-patient confusion and privacy exposure.

options.text: Decompose by data boundary: process each patient record independently, extracting all 12 indicators for that record as structured output.
options.why: Records are independent natural units that fit in context, and per-record structured extraction keeps each call focused and auditable per patient.

options.text: Let a single agent read records in whatever order it chooses until it is confident of the network-wide totals.
options.why: Unbounded autonomy over 2,000 records is slow, unreproducible and provides no guarantee that every record was examined.

options.text: Compute the network-wide totals in code from the per-record structured outputs rather than asking the model to aggregate.
options.why: Aggregation is deterministic arithmetic; doing it in code is exact, cheap and auditable, whereas model-side counting over thousands of items is error-prone.

options.text: Process records in prompts of 500 records at a time so the model can spot trends across patients while it extracts.
options.why: Large mixed batches degrade per-record accuracy and blur patient boundaries; trends belong in the aggregation layer, not the extraction call.

explanation: Partition along the natural data boundary (one record per call), extract structured facts per unit, and leave counting and aggregation to deterministic code. Model-side aggregation over thousands of units is neither reliable nor auditable.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (parallelization); Claude docs — Structured outputs

stem: A retailer's returns-triage pipeline was decomposed into 14 chained Claude calls, each doing one micro-step (detect language, extract order ID, extract reason, classify reason, check policy, and so on). End-to-end latency is now 40 seconds, small errors in early steps compound, and the team spends most of its time maintaining 14 prompts. Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Parallelise all 14 steps so they run at once and the end-to-end latency drops to that of the slowest single step.
options.why: Most of the steps depend on the previous step's output (you cannot classify a reason before extracting it), so they cannot run in parallel.

options.text: Merge steps that share an input and need no validation between them into single structured-output calls, keeping a gate only where a programmatic check adds value.
options.why: Decomposition is a tool, not a goal; steps are worth separating when each is genuinely hard or a check between them catches errors, and over-splitting adds latency, cost and compounding error.

options.text: Replace the chain with a single autonomous agent that decides at runtime which of the 14 steps to run for each return.
options.why: An agent choosing among micro-steps adds planning turns to an already slow pipeline and does not fix the underlying over-fragmentation.

options.text: Add a retry with exponential backoff and a per-step timeout to every one of the 14 calls, plus a circuit breaker on the slowest steps, so that transient errors stop compounding through the chain.
options.why: The compounding errors are content errors from early steps, not transient failures; retries add latency without improving accuracy.

explanation: Decompose to the point where each step is a task the model does reliably and where an intermediate check is worth its latency, and no further. Over-decomposition multiplies cost, latency, error propagation and maintenance.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (prompt chaining; start simple)

stem: A bank must produce anti-money-laundering investigation reports. Evidence for one case totals roughly 600,000 tokens spread across five source systems; the report must read as one consistent narrative; the regulator requires that every statement be traceable to a specific piece of evidence; and the report must be delivered within four hours. Which decomposition satisfies all four requirements?

options.text: A single call containing all evidence from the five systems with instructions to write the report and cite each source as it goes.
options.why: The evidence volume exceeds any single context window, so this design cannot even run.

options.text: An agent that reads whatever evidence it decides is relevant across the five systems and drafts the report when it judges it has enough.
options.why: Self-directed reading gives no guarantee of coverage or traceability and makes the four-hour deadline unpredictable.

options.text: Decompose by report section, with each section writer receiving all raw evidence from all five systems so that nothing is missed.
options.why: Each writer still receives 600,000 tokens, which does not fit, and independently written sections drift into an inconsistent narrative.

options.text: Summarise each source system's evidence in parallel into structured findings with evidence references, then a single synthesis step writes the narrative from those findings, followed by a verification pass that checks every statement maps to a referenced item.
options.why: Per-source parallel summaries fit within context and meet the deadline; a single synthesis step keeps one narrative; references carried through plus a verification pass deliver traceability.

explanation: Large evidence sets are decomposed along source boundaries into structured, referenced findings; consistency comes from a single synthesis step; traceability comes from carrying references through and verifying them at the end. Each requirement maps to a distinct stage.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (parallelization; prompt chaining); Claude docs — Citations

stem: A retailer's COO sponsors a Claude-based contact-centre assistant with one stated goal: reduce cost per customer contact by 20% within two quarters. The delivery team proposes reporting weekly on average tokens per conversation and on the model's score on a public reasoning benchmark. What should the architect change?

options.text: Add response latency to the weekly report so the COO also sees the performance side of the solution.
options.why: Latency is a useful operational metric but is still not the pillar the sponsor named; adding it does not fix the misalignment.

options.text: Report cost per contact and the deflection or handle-time changes that drive it against the sponsor's baseline; keep token counts as an engineering metric.
options.why: Value must be expressed in the pillar the sponsor owns (cost); token usage and benchmarks are inputs, not the business outcome.

options.text: Keep the proposed metrics, since tokens per conversation is a direct measure of the cost pillar the COO cares about and the benchmark shows the model is capable enough to deflect contacts.
options.why: Tokens are one input to model spend, but the sponsor's cost is per contact and includes agent time and deflection; tokens alone can fall while cost per contact rises.

options.text: Replace the public benchmark score with an internal accuracy score from the team's evaluation suite.
options.why: Internal accuracy is a better engineering metric than a public benchmark but still does not report the cost outcome the sponsor is accountable for.

explanation: Align reporting to the value pillar the sponsor cares about and express it in the sponsor's units with a baseline. Engineering metrics such as tokens, latency and accuracy support the story but do not replace the business outcome.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A SaaS vendor sells an in-product assistant with a contractual SLA of p95 under 2 seconds to first visible output. Two designs pass the quality bar: one uses a mid-tier model with streaming and a compact context and costs about 30% more per request than the other, which uses a larger model without streaming and averages 4 seconds before any output appears. The product sponsor is accountable for the SLA. Which recommendation aligns to the sponsor's value pillar?

options.text: Recommend the larger model, because higher quality is always the safer choice for a customer-facing product and the extra seconds can be masked with a loading indicator.
options.why: Both designs already pass the quality bar; choosing the one that breaches the contractual SLA trades the sponsor's accountable metric for a quality margin nobody asked for.

options.text: Recommend the larger model and ask the sponsor to renegotiate the SLA to 5 seconds with customers.
options.why: Reopening a contractual SLA to accommodate a design choice puts the architecture ahead of the business commitment the sponsor owns.

options.text: Recommend the streaming mid-tier design as the option that meets the SLA the sponsor owns, and show the cost delta as a bounded trade-off.
options.why: Performance SLAs are the sponsor's pillar; the recommendation meets it, and the cost increase is quantified and presented as the price of the commitment.

options.text: Run both designs in production for a quarter and let customer preference decide which one to keep.
options.why: An extended production experiment knowingly breaches the SLA for half of customers and delays a decision the data already supports.

explanation: When two designs both meet quality, the tie-breaker is the value pillar the accountable sponsor owns, here performance SLA. Present the other pillars (cost) as quantified trade-offs rather than letting them silently override the commitment.
reference: Claude docs — Streaming Messages; Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A hospital network's chief medical information officer sponsors a Claude discharge-summary drafting tool under the productivity pillar: clinicians should finish documentation faster without reducing quality. Which two metrics most directly demonstrate value against that pillar? (Choose two.)

options.text: Median minutes from discharge order to signed summary, before and after rollout.
options.why: This measures the clinician time the pillar targets, with a baseline for comparison.

options.text: Prompt-cache hit rate for the summary prompt.
options.why: Cache hit rate is a cost and latency engineering metric; it does not show clinicians finishing documentation faster.

options.text: Number of distinct prompt templates in the solution's library.
options.why: Template count measures the size of the build, not any outcome for clinicians.

options.text: Summaries signed per clinician-hour, alongside the rate of clinician edits per summary.
options.why: Throughput per clinician-hour captures productivity directly, and the edit rate guards against speed gained by shipping poor drafts.

options.text: The model's score on a general medical knowledge benchmark.
options.why: A generic benchmark says nothing about documentation time in this network's workflow.

explanation: Productivity is demonstrated with output per unit of human time and the cycle time of the work itself, paired with a quality guard. Engineering metrics such as cache hit rate, template counts and benchmark scores support delivery but are not value evidence.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A public agency is building a Claude-based system for responding to citizen correspondence. The accountable sponsor is a director measured on the statutory 20-working-day response deadline, which the agency currently misses on 35% of cases. The IT department separately wants the lowest possible running cost. The architect must frame the value case for the executive board. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: Lead with the performance-SLA pillar the director owns (cases answered within 20 days rising from 65% to a stated goal), and present running cost as a constraint with an agreed ceiling rather than as the objective.
options.why: The accountable sponsor's pillar defines success; cost is a real constraint but not the goal, and stating it as a ceiling keeps IT's concern visible without displacing the outcome.

options.text: Lead with cost, since finance-backed arguments are the most persuasive to executive boards, and show the response-time improvement as a secondary benefit if it materialises.
options.why: Optimising for the cheapest design may leave the director's statutory failure unaddressed, and the sponsor who owns the outcome is the director, not IT.

options.text: Present all five value pillars with equal weight so the board can see that the solution addresses efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and SLAs at once.
options.why: Equal weighting hides the decision the board needs to make and dilutes the connection between the design and the statutory problem.

options.text: Frame the initiative as a digital transformation of citizen services to secure a larger budget and broader mandate from the board.
options.why: Reframing a concrete SLA problem as transformation overstates scope, invites scope creep and detaches the case from the metric the sponsor is measured on.

explanation: Identify the pillar the accountable sponsor owns, quantify it with a baseline and target, and treat other stakeholders' pillars as explicit constraints. Spreading the case across every pillar, or reframing it to a more ambitious pillar, weakens the link between design and outcome.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A bank's operations sponsor has one value target for a Claude trade-confirmation matching solution: reduce processing cost. Confirmations arrive throughout the day and must all be matched before the 7:00 a.m. next-day cut-off; a small number of urgent intraday queries from the trading desk need an answer within minutes. Which design aligns to the cost pillar while respecting the operational constraints?

options.text: Process every confirmation in real time as it arrives, using the smallest available model to keep the per-request cost as low as possible.
options.why: Real-time processing of the whole volume forgoes the batch discount even though nothing needs an immediate answer, and downsizing the model risks matching quality for no SLA benefit.

options.text: Process everything, including the intraday desk queries, in a single overnight batch job so the whole workload gets the batch discount.
options.why: Overnight batching for the urgent desk queries breaks the minutes-level requirement the desk has, so it fails an operational constraint.

options.text: Process all confirmations in real time with prompt caching enabled so that the shared matching instructions are billed at the cached rate, and serve desk queries from the same path.
options.why: Caching reduces the cost of the repeated prefix but real-time requests still cost more than batched ones, and nothing in the requirement demands real-time for the bulk work.

options.text: Submit the day's confirmations through the Message Batches API in scheduled runs that finish before the cut-off, with a separate real-time path for desk queries.
options.why: Batches give a substantial per-token discount for work that tolerates asynchronous completion, and the separate real-time path preserves the desk's minutes-level need.

explanation: Aligning to the cost pillar means using the cheapest processing mode that the SLA allows: asynchronous batching for the bulk work with a deadline hours away, and a real-time path only for the small urgent slice. Uniform real-time or uniform batch each violate one side of the requirement.
reference: Claude docs — Batch processing; Prompt caching

stem: A SaaS vendor's board has approved a fixed budget for a Claude initiative explicitly on the basis of "new revenue from AI features". In planning, the CEO talks about transformation, the CFO wants cost savings from the support team, and the engineering VP wants a Claude Code rollout for developer productivity. Every option is technically sound. Which first-phase scope is the architect right to recommend?

options.text: A Claude Code rollout across engineering, measured by pull-request cycle time, because it delivers measurable value fastest with the least product risk and no customer exposure.
options.why: Developer productivity is a legitimate pillar, but it is not the transformation outcome the board funded; fast value in the wrong pillar does not honour the funding decision.

options.text: A customer-facing AI feature in the product, measured by attach rate and incremental revenue, with cost and support deflection tracked as secondary metrics.
options.why: The board's funding condition defines the value pillar (transformation: new revenue); the scope and its metric align to that pillar while other pillars are tracked as constraints.

options.text: A Claude-based support assistant, measured by cost per ticket, since the CFO controls the release of the budget and will need to see savings.
options.why: The CFO's pillar is efficiency, but the board's funding condition was new revenue; delivering cost savings would leave the funded objective unmet.

options.text: All three initiatives at one-third scale each so that every executive's pillar is represented in the first phase.
options.why: Splitting a fixed budget three ways underfunds each initiative and makes it impossible to demonstrate the revenue outcome the board asked for.

explanation: Align the first phase to the pillar that the funding decision was made on, and turn the other executives' pillars into tracked secondary metrics or constraints. Spreading scope across every pillar, or picking the fastest-to-deliver pillar, breaks the link between the solution and the business value that justified it.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations
